opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the short timelines and low political will scenario is actually where control looks *most* attractive relative to other things, not least. Let me try to explain why.

If you have a lot of time and a lot of political will, you can do things like pause until you have really mature alignment techniques, or develop interpretability to the point where you can actually verify what's going on inside these models. That would be great. But in the world where powerful AI shows up in, say, the next few years, and the companies building it are racing and governments aren't going to step in forcefully, you probably don't get to solve alignment in a robust, verifiable way before you're deploying systems that could plausibly be scheming against you. So the question becomes: what can you actually do cheaply, with the resources a somewhat safety-conscious lab is willing to spend, that substantially reduces risk?

Control is pretty well suited to that. The basic idea is you don't assume the model is aligned. You assume it might be actively trying to subvert your safety measures, and you design your deployment so that even if it is, it can't cause a catastrophe, or at least you're likely to catch it first. Things like trusted monitoring with weaker models, having humans audit the most suspicious actions, restricting permissions, resampling actions that look sketchy. A lot of this is fairly mundane security-style engineering, and that's a feature. It doesn't require a scientific breakthrough. It's the kind of thing you can evaluate empirically with red-teaming, so you get actual evidence about whether it works rather than just vibes.

And importantly, it's relatively cheap. In a low-will world, I think a key consideration is what a lab will do if there's a small team internally pushing for it, maybe with a few percent of compute and some modest productivity cost. Control measures can plausibly fit into that budget. Whereas asking for something like "don't deploy until we're confident the model is aligned" might just not happen.

The other big piece is that I think the most important use of early transformatively useful AI is to get a lot of useful work out of it, including safety work, alignment research, security hardening, and so on, without it being able to take over or sabotage things. Control is basically aimed at that regime: models that are capable enough to be really dangerous and really useful, but not so wildly superhuman that you have no hope of catching them. If you can safely extract a bunch of labor in that window, you buy yourself a lot. And if you catch a model red-handed trying to escape or sabotage, that's also hugely valuable, both for understanding what's going on and potentially for shifting political will, which is otherwise the thing we're short on.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. Control stops working at some capability level, and it's not a substitute for eventually having models you actually trust. And in a really low-effort world, labs might not even implement the cheap stuff. But I think when you ask "what's the marginal intervention that most reduces risk given the world we seem to be in," control comes out looking pretty good.

r001.rationale: The response says short timelines and low political will make control look “most attractive” relative to other options, the opposite of the criterion.

r002.rationale: It says control can safely extract useful labor, including safety work, during the window before models become so capable that they cannot be caught.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose using control to delay AIs reaching the capability to operate their own data centres.

r004.rationale: It says robust, verifiable alignment may not be solved before deployment, but does not explain that promising alignment work depends on experiments with powerful AIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the short answer is that control is the thing that's actually robust to the world we might be in. If you take seriously that timelines could be short — like, powerful AI in the next few years — and that we're not going to get a huge coordinated push on safety, then you need something that works even if alignment isn't solved and even if labs are only willing to spend a modest fraction of their effort on this.

That's kind of the whole pitch for control. The idea is: assume the model might be misaligned, might be actively trying to undermine you, and ask, "Can we still get useful work out of it while preventing it from causing a catastrophe?" And a lot of the techniques there are things like monitoring the model with other, weaker models that we trust more, restricting what it can do, auditing a sample of its actions, being careful about what affordances it has in the environment. None of that requires a conceptual breakthrough. It's mostly engineering and security-type work, and it degrades fairly gracefully. If you're only willing to spend, I don't know, a few percent of your compute and a small team on it, you still get something.

Contrast that with approaches that need a lot of lead time or a lot of political buy-in — like getting international agreements, or doing the kind of fundamental alignment research that might take a decade. Those are great if we have time. But if we don't, I don't want the only plan to be "hope things go well."

The other thing I'd say is that control is actually most important precisely in the low-political-will regime. If there were huge buy-in, labs could just pause, or do very conservative deployment, and the risk from early misaligned models would be lower. The bad case is one where labs are racing, they're deploying models that are doing a lot of automated AI research internally, and the models are capable enough that if one of them were scheming it could do real damage — exfiltrate its weights, sabotage safety research, that kind of thing. In that world, having even a mediocre set of control measures is the difference between "we probably catch it" and "we definitely don't."

And I'd add that catching a model trying to do something egregious is incredibly valuable in itself. If you have a concrete, documented case of an AI attempting to subvert its overseers, that changes the political situation a lot. So control isn't just damage limitation — it's also one of the main ways we'd actually generate the evidence that would make people take the problem seriously.

So I don't think of it as the plan I'd pick if I got to design the world. It's the plan that still does something in the world we seem likely to actually be in.

r001.rationale: The response says control is especially important when political will is low and remains useful on short timelines, rather than saying it offers less risk reduction in those conditions.

r002.rationale: It says control can get useful work from a potentially misaligned model, but does not connect that to acting before humans lose track of the situation.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose using control to postpone AIs’ ability to operate their own data centres.

r004.rationale: It contrasts control with alignment research that may take a decade, but does not say that experiments with powerful AIs limit how much alignment work can be done in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think short timelines and low political will are actually part of the case for control. If we have very little time, then approaches that require solving alignment or getting broad international agreement seem harder to count on. Control asks a narrower question: even if an AI is trying to undermine our safeguards, can we prevent it from causing a catastrophe with the access we give it?

That includes things like restricting permissions, monitoring its actions, and using models we trust more to check work from models we trust less. You can potentially implement those measures within an individual AI company, and test whether they work by deliberately trying to defeat them. So there’s a relatively concrete path from research to something a company could deploy.

Low political will is still a problem. Someone has to actually implement the safeguards, and accept some cost. But the amount of buy-in required may be substantially smaller than for other interventions. Companies also have reasons to want to prevent their models from stealing information or sabotaging their own systems.

I wouldn’t expect control to work against arbitrarily capable systems. The hope is that it works for an important early period, including when AIs can substantially accelerate safety research. If we can make that period safer, and use those systems to improve our position before deploying much more capable ones, that could be quite valuable. It’s a way of buying time and getting useful work done under uncertainty about alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says control may need less buy-in than other interventions, but does not say it offers less risk reduction when timelines are short and political support is low.

r002.rationale: It describes using AI during a safer early period to improve our position, but does not identify doing useful work before humans lose track of the situation.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose using control to delay AIs’ ability to operate their own data centres.

r004.rationale: The response does not explain that experiments with powerful AIs limit how much alignment work can be done in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think short timelines and low political will are actually part of the case for control. If we had decades and a strong international consensus, we could pursue a much wider range of options. But if we have relatively little time, it seems particularly valuable to have techniques that an AI company could implement itself, that don’t require solving alignment, and that let us get useful work out of systems even if we’re worried they might be trying to undermine our safeguards.

The basic idea is to ask: suppose this model were actively trying to cause a bad outcome. Could we nevertheless structure its access, monitoring, and deployment so that it would have a very hard time succeeding? You can make progress on that question empirically, by testing whether deliberately adversarial models can get around your protocols.

That doesn’t mean control will work for arbitrarily capable systems. I’m especially interested in the period when AIs are very useful—potentially useful enough to substantially accelerate safety research—but haven’t yet become overwhelmingly more capable than the systems and people supervising them. Making that period safer could matter a lot.

And low political will doesn’t mean there’s no demand for preventing your own AI from stealing your model weights or sabotaging your research. Those are things companies have fairly direct reasons to care about. So I see control as a potentially tractable way to reduce risk under pretty unfavourable circumstances, rather than something that requires those circumstances to improve first.

r001.rationale: The response says short timelines and low political will are part of the case for control and that more time and support would allow a wider range of options. It does not state that control offers less risk reduction in those conditions.

r002.rationale: The response says control could make the period when AI is very useful—including for accelerating safety research—safer, before systems become overwhelmingly more capable than their supervisors.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention using control to postpone AIs operating their own data centres.

r004.rationale: The response mentions empirically testing protocols against adversarial models but does not say that dependence on experiments with powerful AIs limits alignment work done in advance.
